question: Define and explain the concept of centre of mass in relation to forces.
markScheme:
3 marks from:
- Centre of mass is the unique point of an object where its weight can be considered to act.
- For an object of uniform shape and density, the centre of mass is the same as the centre of the shape.
- If a force is applied through the centre of mass (concentric force), the body moves in a straight line/linear motion.
- If a force is not applied through the centre of mass (eccentric force), rotation/angular motion is produced.
Max 3 marks.

question:
Explain how a judoka can best maintain stability during a grip fight (kumi-kata) before attempting a throw.

(AO1 = 2 marks, AO2 = 3 marks, AO3 = 3 marks)
markScheme:
AO1 - Identify factors affecting stability (up to 2 marks):
- Stability is the ability to maintain balance/equilibrium.
- Factors: height of centre of mass; area of base of support; position of the line of gravity; mass of the performer (if moving).
AO2 - Application to the judoka (up to 3 marks):
- Lower centre of mass means more stability, so the judoka bends the knees/lowers the hips.
- Wider base of support means more stability, so the judoka widens their stance.
- Line of gravity closer to the centre of the base of support increases stability.
- Greater mass increases stability, relevant when resisting an opponent's pull.
AO3 - Analysis (up to 3 marks):
The base of support is the area beneath the judoka that includes every point of contact with the mat. A wider stance (feet apart) increases the base of support, increasing stability against an opponent's attempts to unbalance them (kuzushi). Lowering the centre of mass by bending the knees and hips brings it closer to the base of support, further increasing stability. Keeping the line of gravity within the base of support, even as the opponent applies force, allows the judoka to resist being thrown. Credit other relevant explanations linked to the judoka scenario.
Max 8 marks.

question:
An archer is shown standing at full draw, in a stable position, ready to release an arrow.

Explain how the musculoskeletal and neuromuscular systems assist the archer in maintaining stability.

(AO1 = 2 marks, AO2 = 3 marks, AO3 = 3 marks)
markScheme:
Indicative content, marked holistically using the levels below.
AO1: biomechanical factors affecting stability (lower centre of mass = more stability; wider base of support = more stability); musculoskeletal system (muscle attachment to bones/joints allows stable positioning); neuromuscular system (isometric muscle contraction, brought about by motor unit recruitment, maintains a stationary stable position).
AO2: application to the archer — feet positioned shoulder-width apart to widen the base of support; body weight evenly distributed and centred over the base of support; core and leg muscles contract isometrically to hold the stable stance while the upper body draws the bow.
AO3: analysis — the base of support is the area beneath the archer including all points of contact with the ground; a wider stance between the feet increases stability against the pulling force of the bowstring; isometric contraction of the postural muscles (e.g. erector spinae, core, quadriceps) holds the body still, recruiting motor units according to the all-or-none law, with force varied through spatial summation; fewer motor units are needed to hold this stationary position compared with a moving action.
Band 4 (7-8): Detailed, accurate, well-linked analysis across AO1/AO2/AO3.
Band 3 (5-6): Good knowledge and mostly accurate application/analysis.
Band 2 (3-4): Basic knowledge, limited application/analysis.
Band 1 (1-2): Very limited/isolated points.
0 marks: No relevant content.
Max 8 marks.

question: Identify the forces labelled X and Y that act on a cyclist during a race, where X acts vertically downward and Y acts to oppose the direction of travel.

question: A gymnast holds a handstand position during a floor routine. State two factors that affect the stability of the gymnast holding a handstand.
markScheme:
2 marks from:
- Height of the centre of mass of the gymnast.
- Area of the base of support (the hands).
- Position of the line of gravity relative to the base of support.
